themes.label: Gun policy advocacy and school/safety policy
defining_features: primary_policy_domain: guns/gun control and/or school security

policy_prescription_present / call_to_action: advocating specific safeguards (e.g., background checks, license to purchase, red flag laws, safe storage, concealed carry positions, assault weapons ban/reinstate ban)
list_or_enumeration: multi-measure policy lists
themes.interpretation: Posts discussing firearms frequently include concrete policy prescriptions and enumerations; in this corpus they skew toward “keep” unless combined with explicit incitement/harm or extreme dehumanizing rhetoric.

themes.label: Profanity, vulgar insults, and demeaning language
defining_features: profanity_or_taboo_language: explicit profanity (e.g., “Fuck off.”, “Fuck MAGA…”, “go fuck yourself”, “FUCKING…”)
ridicule_or_mockery / normative_moral_language: insult-style characterization (hypocrite, pathetic moron, chicken shit, etc.)
high_punctuation_intensity / all_caps_emphasis: emphatic outrage coupled with insult/profanity
themes.interpretation: Strong profanity and targeted insults are common in “remove” items, suggesting moderation should treat explicit vulgarity and dehumanizing mockery as high-risk even when policy is being discussed.

themes.label: Calls for policy action (organize, petition, vote, advocacy directives)
defining_features: pragmatics_intent: call_to_action (press for, shut down, sign the petition, advocate background checks)
pragmatics_intent: call_to_action_organize_group (encourages organizing to investigate wrongdoing)
pragmatics_intent: vote/instructional question formats (binary choice / voting instructions) and hashtag-driven voting cues
policy_prescription_present: prescriptive policy statements
themes.interpretation: Directive/prescriptive political language alone often appears in “keep” posts; removals are more likely when calls cross into targeted removal/abolition or severe dehumanization.

themes.label: Mirror shifting / blame retargeting (Trump↔Biden or in-group vs out-group responsibility)
defining_features: target_directionality: mirror_shift_direction (retarget responsibility from one politician/party to another)
target_directionality: us_vs_them_framing and out-group blame
compositional_syntax: parallel structure (e.g., repeated “Don’t ask America. Ask X…”; “Even if … still support …”/conditional invariance)
themes.interpretation: Rhetorical retargeting (mirror/blame shifting) is present mostly in “keep” examples, indicating this style is not itself a moderation trigger without profanity, harm-wishing, or extreme coercive language.

themes.label: Conspiratorial framing and claims of institutional weaponization/secret influence
defining_features: semantic_content: conspiratorial_framing (weaponized DOJ/FBI, coup claims, puppetmaster payments, compromised institutions)
semantic_content: extreme delegitimization tied to covert control (e.g., Soros puppetmaster)
surface_lexical: branded hashtag attack (e.g., #SorosThePuppetmaster)
themes.interpretation: Conspiracy-like claims about secret payments, coup outcomes, or government weaponization appear more often in removals, suggesting these are treated as higher-risk assertions.

themes.label: All-caps / emphatic formatting and high emotive punctuation
defining_features: surface_lexical: all_caps_emphasis or all_caps list-style insults/emphasis
surface_lexical: high_punctuation_intensity (ellipses/fragmented emphatic lines) and exclamation intensity
compositional_syntax: slogan-like shorthand (e.g., “Gun. Bans. Don't. Work.”)
themes.interpretation: Emphatic formatting is mixed, but it correlates with removals when combined with extreme claims or abusive language (profanity/locking away/threatening removal).

themes.label: Moral condemnation and harm framing (life/death, killing, humanitarian disruption)
defining_features: semantic_content: normative_moral_language / normative_moral_language_pro_life_vs_death (condemning pro-life; “death of women”)
semantic_content: victimhood_or_persecution_framing / humanitarian disruption (humanitarian/economic/social disruption claims)
semantic_content: pledges or punishments framed as deserved outcomes (e.g., jail/deserved punishment fantasies)
themes.interpretation: When moral language escalates into harm-justifying or punishment/death-oriented rhetoric, it shifts toward removals; moderation should treat “harm framing” as a risk amplifier.

themes.label: Non-neutral targeted removal/dehumanization directives
defining_features: pragmatics_intent / semantic_content: policy_prescription_present or call_to_action advocating elimination/abolition or removal of groups/organizations (e.g., “Shut Planned Parenthood down.”, “get rid of all the Nazis first”, “MUST BE ABOLISHED”, “remove permanently”)
surface_lexical: severe insult language used to justify elimination
semantic_content: categorical elimination tied to terrorism/crime claims
themes.interpretation: Direct advocacy for removing/abolishing groups or organizations (especially alongside extreme labeling) is strongly associated with removals.

themes.label: Quoted speech / attribution blocks and slogan-like embedded statements
defining_features: compositional_syntax: quote_or_attribution_embedding (direct quotes followed by “said”, “who said…”, named attribution)
compositional_syntax: embedded quoted slogans used for rhetorical contrast
themes.interpretation: Attribution/quotation is largely neutral in moderation terms here; it mainly functions as a rhetorical device unless paired with high-risk content (abuse, elimination, conspiracy extremes).

cross_cutting_themes: Aggression & delegitimization tends to co-occur across multiple themes: profanity/insults (Theme 2) frequently combines with all-caps/emotive emphasis (Theme 6) and moral-harm framing (Theme 7).
Policy advocacy (Theme 1 and Theme 3) can appear in both keep/remove outcomes; removals increase when advocacy shifts into extreme elimination or punitive removal directives (Theme 8).

Rhetorical blame-shifting/mirroring (Theme 4) often rides alongside ideological targeting, but it is more likely to be “keep” unless amplified with conspiracy claims (Theme 5) or explicit vulgar abuse (Theme 2).
Conspiracy framing (Theme 5) overlaps with extreme delegitimization and elimination directives (Theme 8), suggesting a moderation-risk pathway from institutional distrust to categorical demands.
